# A Field Map and How to Read This Book {#sec-field-map}

By the end of this chapter a reader can place any topic in the book on a single
map, say which parts of that map are settled and which are still argued over,
and read the rest of the book design-first: asking of every component why it has
the shape it has, not merely what it does. The chapter also says plainly where
this book sits next to the comprehensive titles already on the shelf, and what
white space it is written to fill.

## The map

@sec-whole-stack walked one task from raw data to a deployed agent in a single
pass. This chapter zooms out from that vertical slice to the whole field and
shows how the nine substantive parts, Part I through Part IX, interlock. The
spine is the lifecycle of a capability read as a stack: compute and data at the
bottom, a governed behavior at the top, and at every layer a set of choices that
the layer below constrains and the layer above inherits.

```{mermaid}
flowchart BT
  P1["Part I<br/>Foundations and Pretraining"]
  P2["Part II<br/>Adaptation and Alignment"]
  P3["Part III<br/>Reasoning and Test-Time Compute"]
  P4["Part IV<br/>Inference and Serving"]
  P5["Part V<br/>Orchestration"]
  P6["Part VI<br/>Evaluation"]
  P7["Part VII<br/>Infrastructure and Systems"]
  P8["Part VIII<br/>Safety, Interpretability, Governance"]
  P9["Part IX<br/>Ecosystem and Economics"]

  P7 --> P1
  P1 --> P2
  P2 --> P3
  P1 --> P4
  P3 --> P5
  P4 --> P5
  P5 --> P6
  P6 -.feedback.-> P2
  P8 -.constrains.-> P2
  P8 -.constrains.-> P5
  P9 -.prices.-> P1
  P9 -.prices.-> P4
```

A solid arrow points from a layer up to the layer built on it, and the dashed
arrows are cross-cutting forces that reach across layers rather than feed one
into the next. Part VII, the accelerators, the networks, and the data
infrastructure, sits at the bottom: it is drawn below Part I because a cluster's
shape is the first constraint on what can be trained at all (@sec-accelerators-networking,
@sec-orchestration-data-infra). Part I turns that compute into a base model
through scaling laws, data curation, tokenization, architecture, and training at
scale (@sec-scaling-laws, @sec-data-curation, @sec-tokenization,
@sec-transformer-architecture, @sec-moe-ssm-hybrids, @sec-training-at-scale).
Part II adapts the base model to follow instructions and to human preference
(@sec-sft-peft, @sec-rlhf, @sec-dpo-variants, @sec-synthetic-data). Part III
teaches it to spend test-time compute on reasoning (@sec-eliciting-reasoning,
@sec-training-to-reason, @sec-inference-time-scaling). Part IV is the serving
problem: turning a trained model into tokens a user can afford to wait for
(@sec-serving-problem, @sec-memory-scheduling, @sec-faster-decoding,
@sec-quantization-kernels, @sec-structured-long-context). Part V composes served
models into agents with memory, tools, retrieval, and context
(@sec-agent-architectures, @sec-memory-systems, @sec-the-harness,
@sec-multi-agent-systems, @sec-rag-retrieval, @sec-context-engineering). Part VI
measures whether any of it works (@sec-benchmarks, @sec-judging-holistic,
@sec-evaluating-agents). Part VIII reaches sideways into every layer to ask
whether the behavior can be understood, overseen, and secured
(@sec-interpretability, @sec-oversight-control, @sec-security-authorization).
Part IX prices the whole thing and surveys who builds what (@sec-model-landscape,
@sec-tooling-ecosystem, @sec-economics).

The dashed arrows are the reason to read in order. Evaluation feeds back into
adaptation: a benchmark or a judge that moves changes what the next round of
post-training optimizes for. Safety constrains adaptation and orchestration
rather than sitting at the end as a coat of paint. Economics prices pretraining
and serving, and that price reaches up the stack to change design choices that
look, locally, like pure modeling decisions.

## What is settled and what is contested

A field map is only useful if it marks the solid ground separately from the
swamp. Some of this book is settled engineering. The transformer block, the
autoregressive next-token objective, attention with a key-value cache,
mixed-precision training, and the basic fact that loss falls as a smooth power
law in compute are no longer in dispute; they are the shared substrate every lab
builds on. A reader can learn them as one learns the memory model of a language:
as the rules of the game.

Much of the frontier is not settled, and the book marks those places rather than
papering over them. The compute-optimal ratio of tokens to parameters is a
budget-and-deployment-dependent choice, not a constant (@sec-scaling-laws).
Whether reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards teaches genuinely new
reasoning or only sharpens what pretraining already put there is argued in
@sec-training-to-reason. Whether sparse autoencoders are the right primitive for
reading a model's internal features, or a convenient but lossy lens, is open in
@sec-interpretability. Whether a benchmark number or the harness that runs it is
the thing actually being measured runs through @sec-benchmarks and
@sec-evaluating-agents. The signature of the book is that these live debates get
a box, with named positions, instead of a confident sentence that hides the
disagreement.

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested
The deepest open questions cluster in the upper and outer layers of the map, and
they are exactly the white space this book is written to occupy. Three are worth
naming now. First, interpretability has no agreed primitive: sparse autoencoders
gave the field a tractable handle on superposition, but whether the features they
recover are the model's real computational units or an artifact of the method is
unresolved, and @sec-interpretability treats it as open. Second, the source of
reasoning gains is contested: @sec-training-to-reason weighs the claim that
reinforcement learning elicits latent capability against the claim that it
installs new capability, because the two imply different research bets. Third,
agent architecture has no settled form: whether long-horizon competence comes
from better memory systems (@sec-memory-systems), a stronger single-agent harness
(@sec-the-harness), or genuine multi-agent decomposition
(@sec-multi-agent-systems) is an empirical question the field has not closed.
Treat any confident answer in these three areas as a position, not a fact.
:::

## How this book is positioned

Three comprehensive books already cover much of this territory well, and this
book is written to complement them rather than to repeat them. Naming them
precisely is the fastest way to say what is new here.

Chip Huyen's *AI Engineering* (O'Reilly, 2025) is the application layer done
thoroughly: how to build products on top of foundation models you call rather
than train, covering evaluation, prompt and context design, retrieval, and
deployment from the perspective of an engineer adapting models to a use case. It
treats the model largely as a given and asks how to build well around it.

Sebastian Raschka's *Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch)* (Manning, 2024)
is the laptop-scale build: it implements a GPT-style model end to end in PyTorch,
from tokenization through attention to pretraining and fine-tuning, so a reader
understands the machine by constructing a small one. Its gift is mechanical
clarity at a scale one person can run.

Suhas Pai's *Designing Large Language Model Applications* (O'Reilly, 2025) is the
broadest of the three, a holistic tour from the ingredients of a language model
through fine-tuning, retrieval, and agents. It covers a wide surface, and by
design it is lighter on the parts that only appear at frontier scale: at-scale
distributed training, the internals of a production serving stack, and
mechanistic interpretability.

The white space those three leave open is the middle and lower stack at frontier
scale. This book runs whole-stack, from the cluster to the agent, and spends its
depth where the others are thin: distributed training across thousands of
accelerators (@sec-training-at-scale, @sec-accelerators-networking), the
internals of serving, what actually happens inside the loop that turns a model
into affordable tokens (@sec-serving-problem, @sec-memory-scheduling,
@sec-faster-decoding), and interpretability as a first-class engineering concern
rather than a research footnote (@sec-interpretability). The aim is not to argue
the other books are wrong anywhere; it is to read the layers they pass over
quickly, slowly and design-first.

## How to read: the chapter template

Every substantial chapter moves through the same arc, and knowing it in advance
makes the book faster to read. A chapter opens with the **Problem**: the
essential constraint the component answers, in terms of latency, cost, memory,
scale, safety, or correctness. It then gives the **Design**: the core idea that
answers the problem and the principle underneath it. **Evolution** traces how the
design got here, which earlier approaches came first and why they were
superseded, through primary sources. **Trade-offs** names what is sacrificed for
what, and where the known gaps are. **Implementation** appears only when a
minimal sketch, a config, or an operational detail clarifies the design, never to
reproduce a file. Each chapter closes with **Further reading**, first-hand
sources first.

Two callouts carry the book's intellectual signature. A *What's contested* box
marks where the field genuinely disagrees, with named positions, as in the box
above. A *Constraint arrow* box marks where a lower layer dictates an upper
layer's choice. These arrows are the payoff of reading the stack in order rather
than dipping into chapters at random, and the next box shows the canonical one.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Constraint arrow
The clearest single instance of a constraint arrow runs from serving up to
pretraining. @sec-scaling-laws decides how large a model to train and on how many
tokens, and read locally that looks like pure training economics: minimize loss
for a fixed compute budget. But if a model will serve an enormous volume of
tokens over its life, the right move is to deliberately over-train a smaller
model far past the compute-optimal point, because training is paid once and
inference is paid forever. The decision is set by the serving cost in
@sec-serving-problem reaching up the stack, not by the training budget alone.
When you meet a choice that looks unmotivated inside its own chapter, look one
layer down: the arrow that explains it usually starts there.
:::

Two motifs recur without needing a callout. The **three loops**, training,
inference, and agentic, are one control structure seen at three timescales: a
weeks-long loop that turns compute into a model, a millisecond loop that turns a
prompt into tokens, and a multi-step loop that turns a goal into actions. The
**capability, efficiency, trust** lens closes many chapters: a technique buys
capability, or efficiency, or trust, and usually trades one against another, and
naming which it buys keeps the comparison honest.

A reader does not have to read strictly front to back. The parts are written to
interlock, so following the solid arrows of the map, pretraining before
adaptation, serving before orchestration, gives the constraint arrows their force
and is the recommended path. Reading by interest is fine too; the cross-references
will point back to whatever lower layer a chapter depends on.
